## Charter
Reduce cognitive surface, not capability. The pm CLI keeps 100% of its features but presents them behind a small noun-verb grammar. This epic is the umbrella for the brainstormed consolidation clusters (each a child item) and the ADR that fixes the grammar rules.

## Grammar principles (brainstorm summary — ADR child formalizes)
1. Noun-first: one top-level command per domain noun (item lifecycle, list, history, package, schema, config, profile, plan, search, ops/diagnostics).
2. Verbs/facets are subcommands or flags, never new top-level commands.
3. Status/type projections are flags (--status, --type), not command variants.
4. Sugar commands (shortcuts, lifecycle aliases) are hidden aliases or package-provided, never core surface.
5. Nothing is deleted: every current spelling keeps working via an alias shim that prints a one-line migration hint (suppressible via config).
6. Contracts are the source of truth: help tiers, completions, MCP tools, and docs are all generated from the same contract table.

## Target surface (~15 nouns)
init, config, schema, profile, package (extension/install/upgrade), create (+meet/event/remind sugar), get, list (all status variants), update (update-many), close (close-many/delete/restore), claim (release/start/pause), item facets (comments/notes/learnings/files/docs/deps/test), history (redact/repair/compact/activity), search (eval), plan, context (next/focus), ops (stats/health/validate/gc/telemetry), contracts, help.

## Relationship to SDK-first epic
Consolidation is implemented on top of the SDK-first primitives (see linked epic under pm-ugqx): command shims become thin SDK calls, which is what makes the alias layer cheap and regression-safe.
CLI surface simplification: noun-verb consolidation to a minimal agent-first command grammar (zero feature loss)

Consolidate the ~60 top-level pm commands into a minimal, predictable noun-verb grammar so agents can operate the full surface from a small command set. Every existing feature and flag survives; removed spellings live on as hidden back-compat aliases. Duplicate check: searched simplify/consolidation/tiered-help/alias items — only closed historical polish (pm-5k2w, pm-rnpb) matched; no open overlap.

Top-level command list fits one help screen (~15 nouns); every pre-existing command spelling still works (hidden alias shims + deprecation notice); contracts/MCP/completions/docs regenerated with zero feature regression; agent token cost of 'pm --help' + contracts measurably reduced; all existing tests pass unchanged (aliases keep old spellings valid)
Shrink the top-level command surface (~60 -> ~15 nouns) without removing any feature or functionality
Agents discover and operate pm with less context; help/contract payloads shrink; fewer wrong-command retries

The command surface has grown command-by-command to ~60 top-level entries (8 list-* variants, 4 history commands, 4 package-lifecycle commands, 3 lifecycle aliases, 3 calendar shortcuts); agents report the CLI is getting too complicated

Target-grammar brainstorm re-run against that surface; the existing partition still covers every command, and this note records the resulting noun table so the ADR can be decided against something concrete rather than a principle.

Proposed twelve-noun target grammar (verbs are shared vocabulary; every current spelling survives as a hidden alias):

1. item — create, copy, update, close, delete, restore, claim, release, focus. Absorbs: create, copy, update, update-many, close, close-many, delete, restore, claim, release, focus, start-task, pause-task, close-task, item. Bulk is a flag (--ids/--where), not a command; owners pm-ik19, pm-eq4x.
2. list — status and filter variants collapse to flags. Absorbs the eight list-* commands plus aggregate via --group-by/--count-by; owners pm-pfqi, pm-xkgq.
3. context — next and focus become verbs of the navigation noun. Absorbs context/ctx, next, focus; owner pm-kcs4.
4. search — search plus eval as a verb (search eval). Owner: retrieval epic.
5. get — get, history read, and point-in-time reads (--at). Read-only single-item projection.
6. note — the annotation facet: comments, notes, learnings, files, docs, deps, append, test. One facet grammar; owner pm-yql1.
7. graph — already a noun with fifteen subcommands; absorbs deps traversal views.
8. plan — already a noun.
9. history — history, activity, restore-adjacent maintenance, redact, repair, compact, verify. Owner pm-tqel.
10. package — extension, package, install, upgrade. Owner pm-tnud.
11. workspace — init, config, schema, profile. Open question owned by pm-npr3: one customization noun or four peers.
12. ops — stats, health, validate, gc, telemetry, eval, test-all, contracts. Owner pm-6apl.

Removed from the default surface entirely (not from the product): completion-* helper entrypoints (pm-szdc), test-runs-worker (pm-lp4j), meet/event/remind moved into the calendar package as create sugar (pm-o3fh).

Ratio: 75 to 12 top-level nouns, with zero capability removed. That is the number the ADR should either accept or amend.

Two grammar rules that make the table learnable without documentation, proposed as ADR content:
- Shared verb vocabulary: the same verb means the same thing on every noun (add, remove, list, show, set, run). An agent that learns one noun can guess the rest.
- Scope precedes verb, consistently: the config family already established `pm config project set <key>`, and the same ordering should hold anywhere a scope exists, so there is one rule to remember rather than a per-command convention.

Acceptance target for the outcome milestone: the core surface renders in one screen, and the golden-transcript replay shows a measured drop in tokens per completed task against the pre-consolidation baseline.

Shared verb vocabulary, drafted 2026-07-25 as the missing half of the twelve-noun table in the prior note. The noun table alone does not make the surface guessable: an agent that learns `pm item update` still cannot predict `pm note add` unless the verbs mean one thing everywhere. This note proposes the closed verb set the ADR should ratify, and it is deliberately small - eleven verbs cover all 76 current spellings.

Read verbs: `show` (one subject, full projection), `list` (many subjects, filtered projection), `find` (ranked retrieval over a query rather than a filter). Write verbs: `add` (append a member to a collection), `set` (replace a scalar or a whole collection), `remove` (delete a member from a collection), `new` (create a subject), `drop` (delete a subject). Process verbs: `run` (execute something with side effects outside the workspace), `check` (evaluate and report without mutating), `fix` (evaluate and repair, always with a dry-run form).

Three rules make the set learnable. First, one verb has one meaning on every noun: `add` never creates a subject and `new` never appends to a collection, which is the ambiguity that makes the current `create` versus `append` versus `--add` split unguessable. Second, scope precedes verb wherever a scope exists, as the config family already established. Third, plurality lives in the noun, never in the verb: `pm item list` and never `pm items list`, so an agent that guesses a plural gets a precise alias hint instead of an unknown-command error.

Mapping the current surface onto this set is mechanical and reveals the real inconsistencies rather than hiding them: `create` becomes `item new`; `update` becomes `item set`; `update-many` becomes `item set --where`; `close`/`claim`/`release` stay as lifecycle verbs on `item` because they are domain transitions rather than generic mutations, and the ADR should say so explicitly rather than forcing them into `set`; `comments`/`notes`/`learnings`/`files`/`docs`/`deps`/`test` become facet nouns under `note`-style facet grammar with `add`/`list`/`remove`/`set`; `validate`/`health`/`stats` become `ops check` variants; `gc`/`normalize`/`history-repair` become `ops fix` variants with mandatory dry-run; `search` becomes `find`; the eight `list-*` spellings become `list --status`.

Two exceptions are worth naming so they are decided rather than discovered. Lifecycle transitions (`claim`, `release`, `close`) read better as verbs than as `set --status`, and they carry side effects that `set` should not imply; the recommendation is to keep them and document them as the one closed set of domain verbs. And `graph`, `plan`, and `history` already carry rich internal subcommand vocabularies that predate this set; the recommendation is to grandfather their existing subcommands as noun-local verbs and require only that new additions come from the shared set, which is exactly what the conformance gate filed as pm-wt43zj can enforce.

Acceptance framing for the ADR: the vocabulary is ratified as data in the contracts table, not as prose in a document, so that the gate can enforce it and the completion, help, and MCP generators can all read the same source. The measurable claim is that an agent given only the noun list and the verb list can construct a valid invocation for a capability it has never seen, which pm-8pnj's transcript replay can test directly by removing help output from the harness.

Surface census extension 2026-07-26: the census has been counting two of three surfaces.

Both prior censuses measured commands and flags. Measured today on the shipped 2026.7.26 build, the third surface is larger than either governed vocabulary:

- 77 top-level commands, contracted in pm contracts, governed by this epic's noun grammar and pm-wt43zj's conformance gate.
- 470 distinct flag spellings across 1,712 declarations, contracted in the flag-contract tables, governed by pm-fs8q9x's one-spelling-per-concept rule and per-command budget.
- 195 distinct error codes, contracted nowhere, governed by nothing. `pm contracts --json | jq keys` returns fourteen keys and not one of them enumerates a code; grepping docs for a representative code returns nothing.

The sequencing consequence for this epic. Consolidating 77 nouns to 12 reduces what an agent must read to find a command. It does not touch what an agent must read when the command fails, and the failure path is where unplanned tokens are spent - an agent that guesses wrong pays the error output plus a retry, and today it cannot pre-learn the taxonomy that would let it retry correctly the first time. Filed as pm-x4nn3z under this epic so the consolidation is measured against all three surfaces rather than two.

Two live defects found in the same review make the argument without needing a hypothetical, and both are the kind that an enumeration exposes on sight rather than by report:

- pm-yqe0mo: the cross-command flag hint caps its candidate list at three with no truncation marker and no relevance ranking, so `pm deps --add` reports that --add is valid on comments, notes and learnings while omitting files, docs and test - the omitted set containing the command actually wanted. Four lines of root cause in commander-usage.ts.

The same shape was already filed once for pm activity (pm-p3x4), which means the generator is a missing envelope rule rather than two coincidences.

Neither is a grammar defect, so neither would have been caught by the noun-verb work; both are surface-consistency defects of exactly the kind this epic exists to eliminate, on the surface the epic has not yet claimed.

| events | history | `history events` (stream is history-derived) or ops |
| graph | graph | stays — first-class noun (pm-96h7) |

| meet, event, remind, cal, calendar | package-owned | builtin-calendar package (pm-o3fh) |
| update, update-many | update | `--all/--where` bulk facets (pm-ik19) |
| close, close-many, delete | close | bulk + destructive facets (pm-ik19) |
| item, comments, notes, learnings, files, docs, deps, append, test, test-all, test-runs | item | annotation facets (pm-yql1); test-runs worker hidden (pm-lp4j) |
| plan | plan | — |

| telemetry, stats, health, validate, gc, normalize, reindex, comments-audit, dedupe-audit, dedupe-merge | ops | diagnostics/governance verbs (pm-6apl) |
| contracts | contracts | — |
| schema, templates | schema | templates = per-type create defaults |
| profile | profile | — |
| merge | merge | stays (git-driver lifecycle) or ops verb |
| changelog | ops or package-owned | generated artifact |
| guide | help | `help guide <topic>` |
| completion, completion-statuses, completion-tags, completion-types | hidden | runtime helpers, never in help (pm-szdc) |
| beads, todos, command-kit, twin, vcs | package-owned nouns | extension commands, not core surface |
| help | help | — |

1. **One concept, one spelling** — the flag lexicon gate (pm-fs8q9x) must be part of the grammar, not a follow-up: grammar freeze without spelling freeze leaves 87-ish concept-variants alive behind flags.
2. **The error surface is part of the grammar** — 195 uncontracted error codes (pm-x4nn3z) are what agents actually parse when wrong; consolidation that only renames success paths misses half the cognitive cost. 3. **Token cost is the fitness function, not command count** — the measurable acceptance target lives on pm-a22j's baseline + pm-cu1i's ratchet: a grammar that fits one screen AND costs fewer tokens per completed task (pm-8pnj transcript replay). 5. **Grammar serves the philosophy** — fewer spellings = less of the agent's context window spent on *operating the tool*, more on *the project's context*. project management = context management applies to the CLI itself.

ADR accept → pm-0z7n shim layer → pm-0mox counters → noun clusters in dependency order (list pm-pfqi first: pure flag projection, zero mutation risk) → claim sugar (pm-eq4x) → item facets (pm-yql1) → history (pm-tqel) → bulk (pm-ik19) → ops (pm-6apl) → package (pm-tnud) → calendar extraction (pm-o3fh) → aggregate (pm-xkgq) → init/config/schema/profile mapping (pm-npr3) → context trio (pm-kcs4) → gates pm-wt43zj/pm-fs8q9x flip from baseline to enforce.

The placement decision should therefore be taken together with a decision about whether one of them is the planner and the other its selector, rather than moving a command and leaving the overlap in place.

**merge — remove from the agent-facing table entirely as a machine-facing integration point.** The driver subcommand is invoked by git with a fixed argument vector recorded in .gitattributes, so renaming or nesting it is a breaking change to every installed clone for no agent benefit, and the install subcommand is a one-time workspace setup step. The honest disposition is that merge belongs to a non-agent tier of the surface rather than to the noun table — exactly the distinction pm-kxci8x owns. This makes the table both smaller and truer.

Net effect if accepted: the noun table gains graph and loses copy, events, normalize and merge, so the canonical agent-facing surface shrinks while shipped capability is unchanged. The tiering decision for merge is the only part that depends on another open item.

value.text:
Simplification is being measured on the smallest of its three axes (2026-07-27 brainstorm, extends the placement proposal rather than replacing it).

This epic's acceptance criteria and its target-surface table are both expressed in nouns: roughly fifteen, one help screen. The 2026-07-26 census then found five core nouns with no home and a placement proposal followed. All of that is right and none of it is what an agent actually pays. Measured today against pm 2026.7.27, the surface an agent must learn has three axes, and the noun count is the smallest one.

Axis one, spellings: 89 top-level entries, 152 commands and 126 actions in the contract enumeration. This is the axis the target table governs.

Axis two, flags: 326 declared flags across 52 contract flag lists. Nothing in the target table constrains this, and it is where the real growth is. Two of the fifteen target nouns already carry more flags than the entire top-level command list has entries: pm create declares enough that its flags-only contract is 5994 bytes and pm update 6721. Consolidating list-open, list-closed and their six siblings into pm list --status moves complexity from axis one to axis two, which is the correct move for discoverability and a null move for the amount an agent must learn unless the flag lexicon is bounded at the same time. That is what pm-fs8q9x exists for, and the sequencing consequence is that a noun consolidation that lands before a flag lexicon can make the measured learning cost worse while making the help screen shorter.

Axis three, output shapes: one per command, and none of them is declared anywhere an agent can read before paying for it. This is the axis with no owner in the target table at all, and it is the one that determines whether the second call an agent makes is cheap. An agent that has learned pm list still cannot predict what pm list returns, so it learns by paying.

The measurement that ties the three together, and the reason this note exists rather than a general observation about complexity: the call AGENTS.md designates for learning the surface, pm contracts --json, returns 125193 bytes, about 31000 tokens, and it is the brief form. It reports command_flags_omitted_reason, schema_omitted_reason and commander_aliases_omitted_reason all set to unfiltered_default_brief, so 31k tokens buys the spellings and neither the flags nor the shapes. Learning the flags for nine core commands costs about 29000 further bytes across nine more calls. The summary form is 5966 bytes. Filed as pm-gmdzaa, which is scoped to the cold-start entry point rather than to the ceiling contract that pm-5t33or owns.

What this implies for the epic, offered for the ADR to accept or reject rather than asserted:

First, the acceptance criteria should state a target on all three axes, because a fifteen-noun surface with 326 unconstrained flags satisfies the current wording while leaving the agent cost roughly unchanged. The existing criterion that agent token cost of pm --help plus contracts is measurably reduced is the right instinct and the right instrument; it is simply not connected to the noun target that the rest of the criteria describe.

Second, the ordering matters and currently runs the wrong way. The migration sequence recorded in the earlier note moves fragments noun by noun, with the conformance gates flipping from baseline to enforce at the end. If the flag lexicon is not bounded before the list family and the lifecycle aliases fold into their base nouns, each fold adds flags to a noun that already has many, and the gate at the end will be asserting a table whose second axis has grown throughout the migration. Bounding the lexicon first costs nothing that the folds need and makes each fold measurable.

Third, the third axis needs an owner before the grammar is frozen. A declared output shape per command is what lets an agent decide whether to make a call, and it is the missing half of the contract that pm contracts already half-provides: the request side is declared, the response side is not. This is adjacent to the projection work in pm-cxr0jb but not the same thing, because an intent projection selects among shapes that are themselves undeclared.

Nothing here changes the placement proposal or the noun table. The claim is narrower: the epic will pass its own acceptance criteria while the thing it exists to fix, that the CLI is too complicated for agents, is only partly addressed, unless the flag lexicon and the output-shape declaration are inside the definition of done rather than beside it.

Usage-weighted consolidation evidence, measured 2026-07-28 over the complete recorded history of this workspace: 40,343 entries across 2,155 streams, 37 distinct recorded ops.

The surface is wide but the usage is extremely concentrated. Cumulative share by op:

  update                  25.83%   cum  25.83
  comment_add             18.65%   cum  44.48
  files_add               15.48%   cum  59.96
  tests_add                7.22%   cum  67.18
  claim                    6.37%   cum  73.55
  create                   5.24%   cum  78.78
  close                    5.21%   cum  83.99
  release                  5.20%   cum  89.20
  docs_add                 3.31%   cum  92.51
  test_run_track           2.01%   cum  94.52
  note_add                 1.62%   cum  96.14
  learning_add             1.47%   cum  97.61
  update_audit             0.77%   cum  98.37

THIRTEEN ops account for 99.4 percent of every mutation this project has ever recorded. The remaining 24 ops share 0.6 percent, and eleven of them have fewer than ten occurrences each across the entire corpus: plan_link_step 4, note_edit 4, comment_edit 3, comment_delete 3, plan_unlink_step 1, note_delete 1, plan_reorder_step 1, plan_approve 6, plan_append_decision 7, history_redact 23, delete 10.

Three consequences for the consolidation design, all of which change the shape of the proposal:

1. The tail is not dead weight to be removed, it is rarely-reached depth. Every one of those low-count ops corresponds to a real capability the user has forbidden removing. So the lever is REACHABILITY COST, not surface count: the eleven sub-ten ops should cost nothing to an agent that never needs them, and should be one predictable step away for the agent that does. That is an argument for depth-on-demand under a noun rather than for more top-level spellings, and it is a measured argument rather than an aesthetic one.

2. The annotation family is the single largest consolidation prize and is currently four separate top-level spellings. comment_add, note_add, learning_add and the files/docs/tests link adds together are 46.7 percent of all recorded mutations. They share one shape: attach a typed payload to an item. They are spelled inconsistently even in the record - files_add, docs_add and tests_add are plural while note_add, comment_add and learning_add are singular. Consolidating the annotation verbs is worth more measured agent traffic than consolidating the entire list-star family.

3. update at 25.8 percent is the catch-all and the single most valuable target for INTENT SPLITTING rather than merging. One quarter of all recorded mutations go through a verb whose meaning is only recoverable by reading its patch. Any relevance, forecasting or analytics mechanism that reads op as a signal gets almost no information from the most common op in the corpus.

Surface census on the same build for the record: pm --help renders 89 top-level command spellings; pm contracts --summary enumerates 75. That 14-command gap is now its own defect and is not a consolidation question - see the enumeration-closure issue filed 2026-07-28.

Method note so this is reproducible and never re-derived by hand: read every .agents/pm/history/*.jsonl, count the entry-level op field. Do NOT grep for op in the raw file - the JSON-patch entries inside the patch array also carry an op key, and a naive grep returns replace 118,975 and add 89,013, which are patch operations and not commands.

Simplification lever, recorded 2026-07-28: the surface an agent must reason about is not only the commands and flags, it is the vocabulary, and the vocabulary contains synonyms that are not synonyms.

Every lever on this item so far has counted tokens of surface — 89 top-level spellings, 326 flags across 52 lists, help enumerating 89 while contracts enumerates 75, the reachability cost of finding a command at all. All of them measure how much an agent must read. This pass measured something different: how many ways an agent can correctly say one thing, and whether the product agrees with itself about what was said.

For the single most common relation in any tracker, one item must finish before another, there are three ways to write it and three different outcomes. A blocked_by row on the dependent is read by the scheduler and by the graph engine. A blocks row on the blocker is read by the graph engine and ignored by the scheduler, and it is the more common of the two on disk, 219 rows against 127. Writing both, which is what an author does the moment they discover the split, makes pm validate report a dependency cycle — verified live this pass by adding the pair and watching graph audit go 11 findings to 12 and a new warning class appear, then reverting. Fifteen dependency-kind spellings are accepted and only depends_on canonicalizes on write; the rest are stored verbatim and canonicalized on read, so the disk and the reader disagree by design.

Why this belongs on this item rather than only on pm-4020c5. The lexicon item owns the decision about what the kinds mean. This item owns the claim that the surface is too complicated for agents, and a choice with three spellings, one silent failure and no diagnostic is exactly that complexity in its most expensive form: the agent cannot discover the difference from help, cannot detect it from the exit code, and pays for it later as a scheduling error attributed to the tracker rather than to the write. Reducing 89 commands to a smaller noun-verb table does nothing about it. Collapsing the ordering vocabulary to one direction removes a real decision from every agent's path without removing any capability, because both spellings express exactly the same fact.

The generalization worth carrying into the noun-verb work: for each relation and each field the surface accepts, count the number of distinct ways to record the same fact, and treat any count above one as surface to be removed rather than flexibility to be preserved. Aliases that map to one stored form are free — that is what pm-0z7n's shim layer provides. Spellings that map to different stored forms with different downstream readings are the opposite of an alias, and the fifteen-kind vocabulary contains at least one such pair today.

Second datapoint from the same pass, on cost rather than vocabulary. The orientation sequence AGENTS.md tells every agent to run before creating work — context --limit 10, search, list-open --limit 20, list-in-progress --limit 20 — costs 16,631 bytes on this 2,172-item tracker, and adding next --limit 5 brings the mandated preamble to 25,532 bytes, roughly 6,400 tokens spent before any work is touched. Root help is another 12,963 bytes if the agent needs to find a command. The same context call in JSON is 10,277 bytes against 7,517 in TOON, 37 percent more, which is the measurable basis for the TOON-first guidance. Owner for the sequence-versus-single-call question is pm-cxr0jb; recorded here because it quantifies the claim this item exists to fix.

value.text:
Surface census 2026-07-29, measured against the live build, and the consolidation thesis that follows from it.

The numbers. 84 top-level commands render 1,792 flag occurrences drawn from 481 distinct flag spellings. Median flags per command is 11.5, mean 21.3, maximum 126, minimum 1. Two hundred spellings, 41.6 percent of the distinct vocabulary, appear on exactly one command. Fifty-four spellings appear on ten or more. The ten heaviest commands by flag count are update-many 126, plan 97, update 84, create 78, list 65, list-all 64, and list-open, list-in-progress, list-draft and list-closed at 63 each.

Discovery cost, three rungs. Root help is 13,075 bytes, about 3,268 tokens. All 84 per-command helps together are 212,496 bytes, about 53,124 tokens. Machine-readable contracts default to 11,843 bytes, about 2,960 tokens, and enumerate 70 commands. A single command's flag contract via contracts --command get --flags-only is 939 bytes. The full machine-readable surface, contracts --full --json, is 1,142,247 bytes, about 285,561 tokens.

Read those together and the discovery ladder is already mostly right. The middle rung is excellent: 939 bytes to learn one command exactly. The entry rung is cheap at 2,960 tokens but enumerates 70 of 84, so fourteen commands are invisible to the only affordable index. The top rung does not exist as a usable artifact: 285,561 tokens exceeds every context window in service, so no agent has ever read the complete declared surface and no agent ever will.

The thesis. The surface is not hard because there are 84 commands. Eighty-four nouns is a shell utility, not a hazard. It is hard because 481 flag spellings encode a much smaller number of concepts, and 200 of those spellings are reachable only by reading one specific command's help, which means they cannot be learned by pattern and must be memorized one at a time. Command count is the visible metric and the wrong one. Reducing 84 nouns to 12 while leaving 481 spellings in place would move the tax rather than remove it, which is the same conclusion the earlier note reached from the reachability angle and which this census now quantifies.

Collapse one, the filter predicate. Eight list-family commands carry 63 to 65 flags each. They differ from one another in a single status literal. Search, next, context, aggregate, duplicates, test-all, update-many and close-many each accept an overlapping subset of the same filter vocabulary, and the subsets are different in ways no rule predicts. If the predicate is declared once as a contract object and every query surface consumes it, an agent learns filtering once. The eight list commands survive as aliases that prefill one field of that predicate, so no invocation an agent already knows stops working and nothing is deleted. The measurable outcome is that the number of distinct filter spellings falls while the number of accepting commands rises.

Collapse two, the item field set. Create declares 78 flags, update 84, update-many 126. That is 288 of 1,792 occurrences, sixteen percent of the entire surface, spent re-declaring one item schema three times. The divergences between the three are exactly what agents trip on and what the gotcha ledger is full of: repeated --ac accumulates on update, --add-ac and --remove-ac exist on update alone, create has no description-file input while annotation commands have --file, and a semicolon inside an acceptance criterion is rejected on one path and irrelevant on another. Those are not independent bugs; they are the predictable result of writing the same field domain three times by hand. One declared field-set contract with per-verb applicability makes divergence structurally impossible instead of merely documented, and it is the precondition for pm-xm7c's batch mutation input to be specifiable at all.

Collapse three, classify the singletons. A flag used by one command is not automatically wrong. A flag used by one command that an agent cannot distinguish from a shared one is always wrong, because the agent's only recovery is to try it elsewhere and read an error. Every one of the 200 singletons should carry a declared disposition: local, with a stated reason it does not generalize, or shared, in which case it is actually shared. That converts a 200-item memorization tax into a 200-row table readable once, and it gives the flag lexicon gate on pm-fs8q9x an unambiguous acceptance target rather than a judgement call per flag.

What this says about sequencing. The list-family fold has been described before as a null move without flag governance, and the census confirms it precisely: folding eight commands into one removes eight rows from a help index and zero spellings from the lexicon. Collapse two and collapse three are the load-bearing work, and both are flag-lexicon work, which places pm-fs8q9x upstream of the visible noun consolidation rather than beside it. The noun table on pm-pbyu remains correct as the eventual shape; it is simply not the first tranche.

Two contract defects the census exposes on the way. The affordable index enumerates 70 of 84 commands, which is the enumeration gap already owned elsewhere, now with a current count. And the complete form is 285,561 tokens, which is not a large payload but an unusable one; a complete surface that no consumer can load is indistinguishable from an absent one, and it should be paged or queryable rather than emitted whole.

value.text:
Simplification extension 2026-07-29: placing the seven spellings that landed after the noun table, and a three-pattern classification that makes the fold mechanical.

Why an extension and not a restart. The ADR pm-pbyu holds the complete spelling-to-noun table with its twelve target nouns, its fourteen permanent bare-verb aliases and its five open rulings. Nothing here revises that table. This note supplies only what the table cannot answer yet, and one new metric.

The surface at build 2026.7.29. Rendered top-level spellings in root help: 87. Commands enumerated by contracts summary: 71. Seven spellings landed after the table was written: workspace, eval, item, duplicates, start-task, pause-task, close-task. All seven enumerate and resolve correctly, so this is not a contract gap; it is a placement gap. It is also the third time the table has been outrun - first by graph, merge, events, copy and normalize, then by workspace, now by these seven - and each time placement had to be re-derived by hand from live help. The recurrence is the argument for the conformance gate: a new top-level spelling with no declared noun placement should fail the check, which turns placement into a build-time obligation instead of a review-time discovery.

A three-pattern classification of the redundancy. Every spelling that is not already a canonical noun-verb pair falls into exactly one of three patterns, and each pattern has exactly one mechanical fold with its own prerequisite.

Pattern A, the value is in the name. Seven list spellings are the same read with a status value baked into the command name: list-draft, list-open, list-in-progress, list-blocked, list-closed, list-canceled, list-all. The fold is one noun with the value moved to a flag. Prerequisite: the flag lexicon, because the fold is a null move while the filter flags disagree on value grammar - status accepts comma-separated values, type and priority reject them, and tag silently matches the literal comma-joined string.

Pattern B, a subcommand flattened into the name. Four history spellings - redact, repair, author-acknowledge, compact - plus reindex and normalize. These already belong to a noun that exists; hyphenation is the only difference between the current spelling and the target. Consolidation is tracked as pm-tqel.

Pattern C, composition shipped as a new spelling. start-task, pause-task and close-task are each two existing verbs run in sequence, and the help text says so outright: claim an item and move it to in_progress; move an item to open and release its claim; close an item and release assignment metadata. These three are the strongest evidence yet that what the surface needs is a declared composition mechanism, not more names. Three composites cost three spellings; the same ergonomic win for any other useful pair costs another one, forever.

Why the classification matters. It converts the single complaint that the surface is too large into three separable decisions with three different prerequisites, and only Pattern C requires machinery that does not exist. Patterns A and B are pure renaming behind aliases and can land as soon as their prerequisites do.

Placement proposal for the seven, as input to the ADR rather than a ruling.

workspace stays a noun. It is the only home for whole-tracker operations and its first verb group, snapshot, is correctly a subcommand rather than a spelling. Carry the durability finding pm-6l2mza with it: the restore verb is the most consequential mutation in the product and currently the least recorded.

eval should not stand alone. It is one measurement of one subsystem, and it belongs with the other two commands that answer some version of is-this-workspace-sound, validate and health. If the ruling keeps it top-level, it should state why a measurement is a noun, because the same argument then admits a top-level spelling for every future measurement.

item needs a ruling before it grows. Today item mutate applies create, update and close atomically, while create, update and close exist as bare verbs doing the same thing singly. Either item is the batch namespace and the bare verbs are its singular sugar, or the bare verbs are the item namespace and atomic application is a flag on them. Both are defensible; having both spellings with neither declared canonical is the failure mode the table exists to prevent.

duplicates is a read over items with a similarity predicate and belongs as a mode of the read noun that owns list and search. Its discoverability matters more than its name, because it is the only surface that satisfies the duplicate-check obligation this repository's own agent rules impose before creating work.

start-task, pause-task and close-task should not be placed. They should be the first consumers of composition.

A fourth simplification axis, new this session. The metric that matters to an agent is not the number of flags but the number of distinct pairs of spelling and concept, which is strictly larger. Proof: --file is item data on create and update, where the value is a linked path stored on the item, and an input channel on comments, notes and learnings, where the value is a file the prose is read out of and the path itself is never stored. Both meanings are the documented recommendation for their own family, and generalising either one to the other fails silently. Recorded in full on the flag-lexicon item. This axis composes with the axis already recorded here - the number of distinct ways to record one fact - and both are counts an agent pays for in learning cost rather than in tokens.

What this note does not change. The twelve-noun target, the fourteen bare-verb aliases and the five open rulings stand. No spelling is proposed for removal, and every current spelling survives as a hidden alias under the lexicon's alias criterion, so the zero-feature-loss constraint is untouched.

Execution blueprint for command simplification

The target is a small noun-first grammar whose permanent concepts are item, context, history, graph, schema, config, package, workspace, test, plan, ops, and help/contracts. Existing bare verbs remain hidden compatibility aliases where shortening is materially valuable. All feature behavior survives; consolidation changes placement and discovery, not capability.

Transition gates: decide the complete placement table in pm-pbyu; ship the alias resolver and migration hint contract in pm-0z7n; migrate command families behind aliases; generate CLI help, shell completion, MCP actions, SDK action schemas, and documentation from the same contract registry; replay old agent transcripts byte-for-byte where compatibility is promised; measure tokens and wrong-command retries before and after; freeze removal policy only after usage counters show an alias is unused.

Token contract: default help is one screen; contracts summary is one bounded row per noun; command-scoped flags are one further bounded call; errors return the attempted intent, the nearest valid spelling, the corrected invocation, and no unrelated catalog. Mutation output defaults to id, status, and changed-field count. Read output is intent-scoped, streamable, jq-safe, and explicit about truncation.

Shell composability remains a first-class acceptance boundary: stable exit codes; stdout contains data only; stderr contains diagnostics only; JSON, TOON, NDJSON, CSV, and table modes preserve information-equivalent fields where claimed; every list supports filtering, projection, ordering, pagination, and streaming without loading the whole workspace.

value.text:
Simplification axis, 2026-07-30: count the number of independent VOCABULARIES an agent must learn, not the number of commands it must choose between

The 07-28 axis counted the distinct ways to record one fact, which is write-side redundancy. This axis is its read-side twin and it measures worse. An agent operating pm must currently hold three non-nested command vocabularies for one capability set: 85 spellings rendered by help, 70 declared by the contract table, 86 in the MCP pm_run action enum plus 28 narrow tool names. Twenty-six spellings exist only in MCP and seven capability families only in the terminal. Learning one vocabulary does not let an agent predict another, which is the actual cost - not the count of any single one.

The multiplication continues inside a single command. One flag name can carry two value domains: --for means a declared read intent on get, list, next and search, and is validated against the context section enum on context, where the two declared intents are consequently unreachable. Paired flags for one concept can carry two grammars: --dep refuses the unprefixed comma form with an explicit message, while --dep-remove accepts it, matches nothing and exits 0. So the vocabulary count is not even stable per command; it varies per flag and per direction of a flag pair.

Consequence for the consolidation plan. Folding the list-star family into list --status was already known to be a null move unless the flag lexicon lands first. This axis strengthens that to a general ordering claim: every noun consolidation is a null move for an MCP-driven agent, because the MCP vocabulary is not derived from the noun table and would keep the pre-consolidation spellings regardless of what the CLI renders. Consolidating 85 spellings into 12 nouns while pm_run keeps its own 86-entry enum produces a fourth vocabulary rather than removing three. The MCP action set must therefore be derived from the same table this epic consolidates, in the same slice, or the epic's own acceptance criterion - that the agent token cost of orientation measurably falls - is unreachable for the transport most agents actually use.

Metric this axis proposes for the epic's evidence table: not the top-level command count, but the number of distinct declared vocabularies (one per surface, plus one per flag whose value domain is not shared across the commands that render it), and the size of the largest pairwise set difference between any two of them. Today those are at least four and 26 respectively. Zero and zero is the target, and unlike a command count it cannot be reached by hiding spellings behind aliases.

value.text:
Simplification axis, 2026-07-30 (evening): count the ways to bound one read, and watch the count grow with every context feature

Prior axes stand. Counting top-level spellings measured the wrong thing, counting independent vocabularies replaced it, and the three-pattern fold explained where the spellings came from. This axis measures the surface an agent must learn to perform the single most common operation in the product: ask for less output.

Measured at HEAD across twenty read commands. Seventeen distinct output-bounding flag spellings exist: --after, --brief, --check-only, --depth, --fields, --for, --format, --full, --limit, --max-items, --no-truncate, --sample-limit, --section, --stream, --summary, --token-budget, --blocked-limit. No two commands expose the same set.

The distribution, flags per command: the four list variants nine each (--after --brief --fields --for --format --full --limit --no-truncate --stream), context eight, search six, get five, next five, deps four, graph four, health four, history three, activity three, events two, contracts two, comments one, notes one, validate one, and files, stats and aggregate zero.

Four asymmetries are worth more than the total.

The budget flag is on three of twenty, and it is on the wrong three. next, context and deps declare --token-budget. list, get and search declare intent budgets, enforce them, and reject the flag with an unknown-option error, so the one surface that can raise a ceiling is absent from exactly the surfaces whose ceilings were measured as unreachable today.

Three spellings mean less on one command. The list family carries --brief and --full and --fields simultaneously, and health carries --brief and --summary and --check-only and --full. An agent cannot infer from the names which one is the smallest, and on health three of the four now produce the same 1,503-byte verdict while the fourth produces 172,990.

--summary exists on four commands and is missing from the four where an agent most needs it: list, get, next and context. It is present on deps, graph, health and contracts.

Bounding dimensions compose without a declared algebra. context alone accepts five of them at once, and get --depth deep --for inspect produces an omitted result while either flag alone produces content. Nothing states which dimension wins when two disagree, so the composition is discovered by experiment.

The axis, stated as a target rather than a count. Consolidation should reduce bounding to one declared dimension set available identically on every read: what to include, how much of it, and in what encoding. Everything else is an alias onto that set, kept permanently for compatibility. The metric is not the total flag count, it is the pairwise disagreement between commands, which is nine at its widest today, and the trend: every context feature shipped in the last month added a bounding flag and removed none. A consolidation that does not stop that trend has not simplified anything, it has renamed it.

Consequence for sequencing. This is the same conclusion the flag-lexicon prerequisite reached from the other direction, and it strengthens it. Folding nouns is a null move for an agent that still has to learn a per-command availability matrix to ask for less output. The bounding set is the smallest self-contained tranche in the whole simplification programme and it is the one an agent pays for on every single call, so it should land before any noun is moved.

Simplification axis, 2026-07-31: count the surfaces on which the product describes itself, then execute each self-description and count how many are true

Prior axes stand and this one composes with them. Counting top-level spellings measured the wrong thing. Counting independent vocabularies replaced it. Counting the ways to bound one read found the tranche that should land first. All three measure the size of what an agent must learn. This axis measures something the previous three assume: that when the product tells an agent how to use it, the instruction works.

The product is unusually rich in self-description, which is a genuine strength and the reason this is measurable at all. Every read envelope can carry a row contract with an executable jq selector. Every unknown-option error carries a recovery bundle naming which commands accept the flag. Every bounded read carries an omission receipt naming the flag that restores what was withheld. A contract table declares the flags of every command. Help is generated. These are the mechanisms by which an agent is supposed to need no out-of-band context, which is the epic's actual goal.

Measured at HEAD across nineteen read surfaces.

The published extraction contract is one expression: .row_contract.row_keys[] as $key | .[$key][]?. Seven surfaces populate row_keys and the expression returns their rows: list, search, history, activity, health, next, context. Four surfaces publish the same expression with row_keys empty — deps, stats, aggregate, get — so it is guaranteed to return nothing; pm deps on an item with eighteen dependency edges returns zero rows through its own published selector. Seven surfaces publish no contract at all: comments, notes, files, docs, graph, contracts, validate. One surface, events, emits no envelope, so no contract is possible and none is documented.

So of nineteen surfaces, the self-description is true on seven, false on four, absent on eight.

The false four are the finding. An absent contract fails loudly: the agent reads null, learns the surface is uncovered, and special-cases it once. A false contract fails silently: the documented one-liner runs, exits zero, and yields an empty stream that is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty result. Every downstream count, loop and guard reads zero and no error is raised anywhere. Silence is the expensive failure mode because the agent does not learn that it needs to look further.

The same shape appears in two other self-descriptions measured today, which is what makes it an axis rather than a defect. The unknown-option recovery bundle names three commands that accept a flag when more than three accept it, capped silently and in arbitrary order, so the hint reads as exhaustive while potentially excluding the right answer — already filed. The graph command family publishes edge_count from four independent counting conventions under one field name, so analyze reports 10,106 edges and centrality reports 7,351 for the same graph at the same cache fingerprint, and an agent comparing them concludes a quarter of the graph vanished — filed today.

The axis, stated as a metric. Not the count of self-describing surfaces, which is already high and rising. The fraction of published self-descriptions that are executable and correct when executed: 7 of 11 for the row contract, and each recovery hint, omission receipt, contract-table entry and generated example independently checkable the same way. Today that fraction is measurable only by hand. The target is that it is measurable by a gate — one that takes each envelope, executes the instruction the envelope itself published, and asserts the result matches what the envelope contains.

Why this belongs to the simplification epic rather than to governance. The epic's acceptance criterion is that the agent token cost of orientation measurably falls. A false self-description raises that cost above the no-contract baseline, because the agent pays for the contract, pays for the failed extraction, and then pays for the fallback it would have taken anyway. Every self-description the product adds is a bet that the agent can trust it; the bet is only worth making if a gate collects on it. Consolidation that increases the number of self-describing surfaces without proving them true is not simplification, it is a larger surface that is harder to distrust.

Consequence for sequencing. This is cheaper than every noun move and independent of all of them, because it changes no grammar and no placement. It also makes the noun moves safer: once each surface's self-description is executable and gated, the alias layer's migration hints and the generated help become checkable artifacts rather than prose the consolidation has to be careful not to break.

Surface-growth measurement and a re-sequencing proposal, recorded 2026-07-31. This note does not restate the twelve-noun table or the eleven-verb vocabulary already held in the notes above; it measures what has happened to the surface while those two proposals waited for a decision, and argues that the measurement changes the delivery order.

The census, on the same methodology as the earlier ones. pm --help renders 87 unique top-level spellings after splitting alias pairs; pm contracts --summary reports 71 canonical command summaries. Against the recorded series in this epic - roughly 60 on 2026-07-05, 64 on 07-06, 65 on 07-07, 67 on 07-13, 73 on 07-18, 75 on 07-25, and the 74-summary/88-spelling split on 07-26 - the trend is monotonic growth of about one spelling per day, and the surface is now roughly 45 percent larger than when this epic was opened. Names that appeared after the noun table was drafted include workspace, item, duplicates, events, merge and history-author-acknowledge. The consolidation target is twelve. The gap is widening.

The token cost of that growth, measured today on the real tracker rather than a fixture: pm --help 13,082 bytes; pm contracts --flags-only 124,288 bytes, up from the 117,070 recorded on 07-26; pm contracts --summary 9,364 bytes; pm context --limit 10 9,218 bytes against the 7.6 KB recorded on 07-24; pm list-open --limit 20 4,734 bytes against 3.6 KB; pm next 9,951 bytes; pm search --limit 20 7,658 bytes. Discovery and payload are both rising, and the ratio is the argument this epic has been missing: an agent now spends more tokens learning that 87 commands exist than it spends operating the roughly twelve it actually needs for the loop AGENTS.md prescribes.

Why the surface grew while consolidation was open, mechanically. A fence does exist. scripts/measure-agent-token-surface.mjs --check fails with 'missing baseline' the first time a new top-level command appears, because compareBaseline compares each measured command against a committed entry and treats an absent entry as a violation. The documented remedy is pnpm quality:token-surface:update, which regenerates the baseline. So the fence is a ratchet log rather than a budget: it records that the surface grew and requires someone to acknowledge it by rerunning a script, with no ADR reference, no grammar-conformance check, and no count ceiling. The baseline's required_commands array is now a 67-entry list of every command ever accepted, and it has only ever grown. The gate passed today, green, across 91 surfaces, on a surface 45 percent larger than when this epic opened. That is the fence working exactly as written and not doing the job the epic needs.

The re-sequencing proposal. The recorded sequence is decision pm-pbyu, then alias substrate pm-0z7n, then independent family migrations, then tiered help pm-e2bq and generated contracts pm-mu8m, then the token regression proof. That order makes the ADR a hard prerequisite for every downstream item, and the ADR has been in proposed state for 26 days while the surface grew 45 percent. The alias substrate is the one piece of that chain which is decision-independent: it is pure mechanism - a table mapping a retired spelling to a canonical invocation plus a migration hint - and it does not require agreement on what the canonical spellings will be. Shipping it first inverts the dependency. The ADR stops being a gate on all work and becomes a choice of table contents, each family migration becomes independently reversible because the old spelling keeps working through the substrate, and the epic can start reducing the default surface before the twelve-noun table is ratified.

Two additions the measurement argues for directly.

First, the growth fence should be denominated in the thing the epic is trying to reduce. Today it counts bytes with ten percent headroom, so several new commands can land inside the slack before anything trips, and the trip is a size complaint rather than a grammar complaint. A count-based ceiling on default-visible top-level spellings, with the ceiling recorded in the ADR and lowered as families migrate, converts each addition into a decision instead of a script rerun. New capability then lands as a verb on an existing noun, which is the constraint pm-plwm already carries for query features, applied to the whole surface.

Second, the done-definition should be measured on payload as well as on help. Every metric this epic currently trends - root help, per-command help, contracts - is discovery cost, and discovery is paid once per session. The 21 percent growth in pm context and the 31 percent growth in pm list-open over seven days are paid on every call, and no baseline in the repository tracks them on a corpus of representative size; the token-budget gate seeds 27 items against a real tracker of 2,231. The one-screen help target should therefore sit beside a payload-per-intent target measured on the real corpus, or the epic can succeed on its stated metric while the cost it exists to reduce keeps rising.

New simplification axis, recorded 2026-08-01. Prior axes stand and none is restated: spelling count, independent vocabularies, ways to record one fact, output-bounding flag spellings, distinct entrypoint targets. This axis measures none of those.

Axis: teachability. For every place the surface can refuse an agent, ask whether the refusal contains what the agent needed to succeed. Count teachable refusals, not commands.

Why this axis and why now. Every prior axis measures the size or the redundancy of the surface, and every one of them says the same thing, which is that the surface is too large. That conclusion is already recorded and is not in dispute. What the size axes cannot tell us is which reductions actually help an agent, because a consolidation that halves the spelling count while leaving every refusal uninformative buys an agent nothing: it still has to leave the tool to find out what is legal. Teachability is the axis on which consolidation can be justified or falsified.

The 2026-08-01 measurement. Fifteen flags with closed value domains were probed with a deliberately invalid value. Thirteen render the complete legal set in the refusal: type filters, priority, both format flags, the create positional type, severity, confidence, dependency kind, risk, graph subcommand, status role, and get depth. Two do not: the field projection selector and the context intent selector. Those two are the flags that exist specifically to reduce output size, so the teachability failure is concentrated exactly where the cost lever is. The intent selector is worse than silent, because it returns one nearest-match guess and points at two help surfaces that do not carry the set either. The field selector's help renders two example values behind the word valid, which reads as a complete two-member domain when the real domain is at least twenty-four.

The consequence for consolidation. A noun-verb consolidation reduces the number of places an agent can be wrong about a verb. It does nothing about the number of places an agent can be wrong about a value, and value domains are where the measured failure is. That means the consolidation programme should carry a teachability criterion alongside its spelling-count criterion, and a consolidated surface that regresses teachability is not an improvement even if it is smaller.

Method note for the next pass, so this is reproducible rather than re-derived. Probe each flag with a value that cannot be legal, capture the refusal, and score it teachable when the envelope names at least two legal values or explicitly names the complete set. Do not score a nearest-match suggestion as teachable on its own: one suggestion tells an agent what to try next, it does not tell it what the domain is, and the difference shows up the moment the first suggestion is also wrong.

Simplification axis (2026-08-02) — count the distinct POSITIONAL SHAPES an agent must learn, not the commands.

Prior axes counted nouns (~60 to ~15), vocabularies (>=4 independent action sets), output-bounding flag spellings (17 across 20 read commands), ways to record one fact, and teachability of refusals. All of them measure the named surface. The positional layer was never measured and has no owner among the four grammar-governance items - pm-fs8q9x owns flags, pm-wt43zj nouns and verbs, pm-hqa8g1 exit codes, pm-x4nn3z error codes.

Measurement at 2026.8.2, 76 rendered top-level commands: 21 distinct positional shapes. 42 commands take no positional. The item id appears as required <id> on 13 and optional [id] on 4 - one concept, two arities, no rule. Subcommand dispatch has five incompatible shapes: <subcommand> [id] [target] (graph), <subcommand> [artifact] [base] [ours] [theirs] (merge), [subcommand] [name] (schema, profile), [subcommand] [id] [stepRef] [reorderTo] (plan), [namespaceOrSubcommand] [subcommand] (telemetry, first slot polymorphic). pm config is [scope] [action] [key] [value], four untyped slots where position alone carries meaning.

The axis has teeth because the notation is not merely varied, it is false: schema, profile and plan render [subcommand] and exit 2 when it is omitted, while telemetry, item, workspace and config render the same notation and accept omission at exit 0. The two commands that declare <subcommand> honestly (graph, merge) refuse with 'Missing required argument subcommand'; the three that declare it optional and are not refuse with 'Invalid argument value' - a different error class for the same condition, pointing the agent at a value it never supplied.

Consequence for the epic's target surface: consolidating 76 nouns to ~15 does not reduce what an agent must learn if each of the 15 keeps its own positional shape. The noun count and the shape count must fall together, so the target-surface table should declare a positional signature per noun, not only a name. Filed as pm-ya7x55 (parent mpbb, implements this epic, blocked_by pm-wt43zj).

Measured cost of the surface for the same date, as the baseline this axis is traded against: pm --help 13,805 B (~3.5k tok); pm contracts default/summary 13,467 B (~3.4k tok, identical - default is already the summary form); pm contracts --full 1,315,441 B (~329k tok, 97.7x); sum of all 76 per-command help payloads 218,207 B (~54.5k tok). The per-command help sum is the true cost of learning the surface once, and it is the number consolidation must move.

Surface axis, recorded 2026-08-02: count the commands whose correctness depends on a repository state the CLI never reports.

Prior axes counted commands, nouns, vocabularies, bounding-flag spellings, self-descriptions, positional shapes, and refusal teachability. This one counts something the surface census cannot see, because the defect is not in the command list — it is that several commands are only correct at one point in a workflow, and no read anywhere in pm says which point you are at.

The class, measured against the installed 2026.8.2 surface: pm merge install (correct exactly once per clone, and a fresh clone or worktree silently has no field-aware merge until it is run), pm merge reconcile and pm merge report (meaningful only while receipts are pending), pm history-repair (documented as the thing to run after a merge), pm validate --check-history-drift (the check whose result is only interpretable if you know whether a merge just happened), and pm health (which aggregates all of it). Six surfaces, one underlying question — is this workspace post-combination-clean, and if not, what is the next correct action — and no single read that answers it. The guidance instead lives in prose: the merge driver prints 'run pm validate then pm history-repair', which is transient stdout, and AGENTS.md carries the fresh-clone rule as a sentence a returning agent has to remember.

Why it belongs to this epic rather than to the concurrency epic: consolidation is the fix. The workflow position is derivable — pending receipts, drift state, driver installation and reanchor points are all recorded — so the honest grammar is one read that reports where the workspace stands plus what to run, not six commands the caller must sequence from memory. That is the same lever as pm-kcs4 (navigation trio under one noun) and pm-tqel (history family under one noun), applied to the family whose members are currently distinguished only by which moment you are in.

Related surface observation for pm-kxci8x, not filed separately: pm merge exposes four subcommands and one of them, driver, exists solely as a git plumbing entrypoint that no agent ever invokes, matching the pm-lp4j and pm-szdc pattern of runtime plumbing sitting in the default agent-facing surface.
